strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark for semantic difference recognition, addressing a real gap: most prior RSD work relies on synthetic, sentence-level augmentations.

Very comprehensive evaluation across a wide range of systems (unsupervised alignment baselines, few-shot and fine-tuned LLMs including reasoning models, and multiple encoder architectures) and three language pairs, with additional Kendall tau, inference-time, position-based, and cross-lingual label-projection analyses in the appendix.

Central empirical finding — a large and consistent performance gap between synthetic iSTS-RSD and naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all model types — is an important and practically relevant result for the MT evaluation/multilingual alignment community, cautioning against over-reliance on synthetic benchmarks.

High transparency: full annotation guidelines, interface screenshots, inter-annotator agreement statistics (including honest reporting of relatively low span-level agreement), and a dedicated analysis of how annotator discrepancies affect system rankings.

Useful qualitative and quantitative failure analyses (e.g., LLM output formatting failures, underlabeling near document ends, degradation with document length) that provide actionable insights for future work.
Data and code are released, and the paper contextualizes annotation agreement against related work (e.g., MQM error span annotation) to argue the agreement levels are within normal range.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement at the span level is quite low (IoU 11–44%, F1 18–56%) with only two annotators per language pair, raising concerns about the reliability of the gold labels underlying the main results; the label distribution is highly skewed (only 10–17% of tokens annotated as differing), which could make Spearman correlation unstable despite the authors' attempt to mitigate this with Kendall tau.

No human/oracle upper-bound performance is reported to contextualize how much of the very low absolute scores on SwissGov-RSD (often single digits) reflects genuine task difficulty for models versus annotation noise or task ill-definedness.
The merging procedure for overlapping annotations (manual selection of 'better' annotations) introduces subjective curator bias that is not fully quantified.

Annotator pool is small (undergraduate students, not domain/translation experts) and language coverage is narrow (three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages paired with English), limiting generalizability of conclusions, as acknowledged in the Limitations section.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD conflates multiple confounds (domain, genre, document length, annotation protocol, naturalness) rather than isolating 'syntheticness' as the sole driver of the performance gap, weakening the causal interpretation of the central claim.

Some experimental choices (e.g., restricting LLM evaluation on SwissGov-RSD to only the best iSTS-RSD performers, per-model augmentation budget differences) reduce the comparability/completeness of certain result tables and are justified mainly by compute constraints.

strengths: Addresses a real and under-studied gap: prior RSD benchmarks (iSTS-RSD) are synthetic/sentence-level, while this work provides a naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual resource sourced from real government translations.

Thorough and transparent documentation of the annotation process, including guidelines, interface, trial/main phases, and multiple inter-annotator agreement metrics (IoU, F1, Spearman on matched spans).

The empirical headline finding—large performance drops from synthetic iSTS-RSD to the naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all model types (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, fine-tuned encoders)—is a useful and actionable observation for the community, particularly the striking overfitting behavior of fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini.

Reasonably broad system coverage (multiple encoder families, open and closed LLMs, reasoning models) and careful secondary analyses (document-length degradation, LLM output-format failures, qualitative error analysis).

Good reproducibility practices: code/data release, explicit prompts and hyperparameters in appendices, and an appendix specifically checking how much conclusions depend on which annotator's labels are used (Appendix A.4).
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is quite low and uneven across language pairs (e.g., EN-DE span IoU ~10-11%, fuzzy-match correlations ranging widely from 66-98%), raising concerns about the reliability of the 'gold' labels used to rank systems; the paper's justification (citing MQM error-span annotation agreement as a precedent) does not fully resolve this, since the current task and scale differ substantially and no human performance ceiling is reported alongside model scores for direct comparison.

The dataset merging process when both annotators labeled a document is subjective ('include the annotations adhering more to the guidelines'), introducing an unquantified source of bias into the final gold set without clear inter-rater adjudication protocol.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD conflates several confounds simultaneously (naturalness, domain, document length, and label distribution skew of 10-17% vs 25-30%), making it hard to cleanly attribute the large performance gap to 'naturalistic vs synthetic' data per se rather than to domain/length/label-imbalance shift.

Limited methodological novelty: the core detection approaches (DiffAlign, token regressor, LLM prompting/fine-tuning) are directly adopted from prior work (Vamvas and Sennrich, 2023); the contribution is primarily a new evaluation resource rather than a new method.

Due to computational constraints, only the single best-performing LLM system per category was evaluated on SwissGov-RSD, limiting the comprehensiveness and fairness of LLM-vs-encoder comparisons on the new benchmark.

Absolute correlation scores on SwissGov-RSD are very low across the board (often single digits), and combined with the annotation noise described above, it is unclear how much headroom exists for genuine improvement versus noise in the gold labels—an important caveat for a paper whose central claim is about a 'considerable gap' between systems and human judgment.

Dataset scope is narrow (three closely related high-resource European languages, Latin script, single domain of Swiss government text), limiting generalizability of the findings, a limitation the authors acknowledge but which still constrains the broader impact claims.

strengths: Introduces the first naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for semantic difference recognition (SwissGov-RSD), filling a genuine and well-motivated gap left by prior synthetic benchmarks (iSTS-RSD).

Very comprehensive experimental scope: unsupervised alignment methods, few-shot prompting, fine-tuned LLMs (open and closed source), and fine-tuned/unsupervised encoder models, including a reasoning-model comparison and a novel LLM-based cross-lingual label-projection strategy for training data.

Strong, actionable empirical finding with clear practical relevance: systems that excel on synthetic iSTS-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini) collapse on the naturalistic SwissGov-RSD benchmark, convincingly demonstrating that synthetic augmentation does not capture real-world distributional properties (domain, length, label skew).

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: detailed guidelines, trial + main annotation phases with feedback loops, quantitative inter-annotator agreement (IoU, F1, Spearman on matched spans), manual adjudication of overlapping/faulty documents, and an explicit appendix analyzing how annotator disagreement affects downstream benchmark conclusions.

Rich supplementary analyses that strengthen the paper's claims: qualitative error analysis (underlabeling near document ends), position-in-document degradation analysis, LLM output-format failure rates, and inference-time/efficiency comparisons across model classes.

High reproducibility: full prompts, hyperparameters, annotation interface description, dataset statistics, and per-language/per-augmentation breakdowns are provided in appendices, alongside public release of code and data.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is quite low for span-level matching (especially EN-DE, IoU ~10-11%), and only 25 overlapping documents per language pair are used to estimate it; while the paper addresses this candidly, the reliability of the gold labels used to draw strong quantitative conclusions (e.g., Spearman correlation comparisons) remains a soundness concern.

Annotators are only two per language pair (undergraduate/bachelor's students), and most of the corpus is single-annotated after the trial phase, limiting the confidence in label quality across the bulk of the 224 documents.

The claim that observed agreement is "within normal ranges" rests on a single comparison to MT error-span annotation (Kocmi et al. 2024), which is a fairly thin basis for validating annotation quality for a newly introduced task/scale.

The dataset is restricted to English plus three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script European languages, which the authors acknowledge limits generalizability of the central claims to typologically distant languages or non-Latin scripts.

The methodological contribution is largely an evaluation/benchmarking exercise using existing architectures (DiffAlign, standard encoder fine-tuning, standard LLM prompting/fine-tuning); no new modeling approach is proposed to close the identified synthetic-to-real gap, somewhat limiting the technical novelty beyond the dataset itself.

The LLM-based label projection for cross-lingual fine-tuning data introduces an additional layer of potentially noisy supervision (validated only via a small 50-sample manual check per language pair), which could affect the fairness of comparisons between EN-only and cross-lingual fine-tuned models.

Given the modest dataset size (224 document pairs per language pair) and known annotation variability, some fine-grained comparisons between closely performing systems (e.g., different encoder variants) may not be statistically robust, and no significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the Spearman/Kendall correlations in Table 3.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior work on semantic difference recognition relied on synthetic, sentence-level benchmarks; this paper introduces the first human-annotated, naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for the task (three EN-X pairs, 224 multi-parallel documents).

Extensive and carefully designed evaluation spanning unsupervised alignment baselines, few-shot LLM prompting, fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned/pretrained encoder models of varying sizes and context lengths, giving a broad picture of the state of the art.

Annotation process is documented in detail (trial phase, guidelines, compensation, quality control via overlap-based IoU/F1/Spearman metrics, replacement of a low-quality annotator), and agreement statistics are transparently reported and contextualized against comparable tasks in the literature.

The central empirical finding — a large, consistent performance drop from synthetic iSTS-RSD to naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all systems and model classes — is a valuable and well-supported contribution that has clear implications for future benchmark design and model development.

Rich supplementary analyses (label-projection quality checks, document-length degradation analysis, inference-time comparisons, Kendall τ-b robustness check) strengthen the credibility and usefulness of the results.
Code, data, and detailed appendices (prompts, guidelines, domain breakdown) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is fairly low (token-level Spearman 43.6–65.1), and for the majority of the dataset only a single annotator's labels are used (adjudication happens only for the 25 overlapping documents per language pair), which limits confidence in gold-label reliability and makes it harder to distinguish genuine model failure from annotation noise/task subjectivity.

The dataset is restricted to three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages within a single narrow domain (Swiss government web content), limiting the generalizability of the reported performance gap to other domains, language pairs, or scripts (acknowledged by the authors as a limitation).

The paper is primarily a benchmark/resource contribution rather than a new method; while the empirical analysis is thorough, the core novelty over related naturalistic comparable corpora (e.g., SwissAdmin, 20min-XD) is the token-level annotation layer rather than a fundamentally new resource type.

Dataset scale (224 document pairs per language pair) is modest for fine-tuning comparisons, and some evaluation choices (heuristic JSON repair, padding/truncating malformed LLM outputs, capping iSTS-RSD evaluation to 100 samples per setting) introduce additional noise that is not fully quantified.

The label-projection approach for non-English fine-tuning data relies on an LLM (GPT-4o-mini) whose quality is only spot-checked on 50 samples per pair, leaving open questions about systematic biases introduced into cross-lingual fine-tuning sets.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely needed resource: a naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition, addressing a clear gap left by prior synthetic-only benchmarks (iSTS-RSD).

Extensive and fairly rigorous benchmarking effort spanning unsupervised alignment methods, multiple open- and closed-source LLMs (including reasoning models), and several encoder architectures (including long-context encoders), under few-shot, fine-tuning, and label-projection settings.

Strong transparency and reproducibility support: detailed annotation guidelines, interface description, prompt templates, per-language statistics, and multiple appendices documenting agreement computation, label-projection quality checks, and inference-time comparisons.

The central empirical finding—substantial performance degradation from synthetic to naturalistic cross-lingual settings, including for models that excel on iSTS-RSD—is a useful and plausible contribution to the community, with supporting qualitative and positional (long-document) analyses.

Careful treatment of inter-annotator agreement, including an explicit comparison with agreement levels reported in related span-annotation literature, and an appendix quantifying how annotator disagreement affects system rankings (showing rankings remain stable).
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is low to moderate (token-level Spearman 43.6–65.1, with one language pair's original annotator discarded for even lower quality, 9.4), raising concerns about the reliability of the gold labels underlying the entire benchmark and about how much of the reported 'poor model performance' reflects task/label noise rather than genuine model weakness.

The annotation task is acknowledged to be highly subjective (Figure 8 shows annotators differing systematically between minimal-span vs. whole-phrase labeling strategies), yet the paper does not explore alternative, possibly more robust, evaluation protocols (e.g., span-level or binary difference detection) that might reduce this subjectivity.

Dataset scope is narrow: only three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script, English-centric language pairs drawn from a single domain (Swiss government text), limiting generalizability claims despite the paper's broader framing about multilingual content alignment.

The overall correlation scores are very low across the board (mostly single digits to low twenties on SwissGov-RSD), which makes it hard to distinguish genuine model capability differences from noise; no explicit human performance upper bound is integrated into the main results table for direct comparison against system scores.

The discussion/results section is largely descriptive (trend reporting) with limited deeper causal or error-type analysis beyond one qualitative example figure and a document-length analysis; the underlying reasons for specific model failures (beyond generic 'LLMs underlabel' or 'overfit to augmentation patterns') are not deeply investigated.

Dataset size (224 document pairs per language pair, used purely as a test set) is modest, and fine-tuning still relies entirely on the synthetic iSTS-RSD/PAWS data augmented with LLM-based label projection, whose quality is only spot-checked on 50 samples per language pair rather than rigorously validated.

strengths: Introduces a novel, naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark (SwissGov-RSD) for a task (RSD) that previously relied only on synthetic augmentations of sentence-level data, filling a genuine gap in the literature.

Very comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning unsupervised alignment baselines, multiple encoder architectures (including long-context multilingual encoders), open- and closed-source LLMs, few-shot prompting, reasoning models, and fine-tuning (LoRA for LLMs, regression heads for encoders), giving a broad picture of the state of the art.

The central finding -- a large, consistent performance drop from synthetic iSTS-RSD to naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all model families -- is a clear, well-supported, and practically important result for the MT-evaluation/multilingual-content community.

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: detailed guidelines, trial + main phases, multiple inter-annotator agreement metrics (IoU, F1, fuzzy/exact span correlation), explicit handling and disclosure of a problematic annotator, and an appendix analyzing how annotation discrepancies affect downstream conclusions.

Additional analyses (label projection quality check, inference-time comparison, performance vs. document length, Kendall vs. Spearman robustness check) go beyond the core results table and strengthen the reliability of the reported conclusions.
Data, code, and detailed prompts/appendices are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is fairly low (token-level Spearman 43.6-65.1, with some subset correlations near zero or negative in Appendix A.4), raising concerns about the intrinsic reliability/ceiling of the task and complicating interpretation of low model scores as reflecting model failure rather than label noise.

The dataset is limited to three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages paired with English (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), and covers only 224 government documents from a narrow set of domains (admin.ch subdomains), limiting generalizability claims.

Only two annotators per language pair with partial overlap (25 of ~110 docs) were used; discrepancies were resolved via manual inspection and merging by the authors, which could introduce subjective bias into the final 'gold' labels not fully captured by the reported agreement statistics.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD conflates several confounding factors simultaneously (domain, label distribution skew, naturalness, document length), so the attribution of the performance gap specifically to 'syntheticness' versus other distributional shifts is not cleanly isolated.

Due to computational constraints, several models (e.g., Llama-3.1 8B few-shot/fine-tuned, GPT-4o-mini few-shot, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) were not evaluated on SwissGov-RSD, weakening the completeness of the main comparison table for the paper's central claim.

Licensing constraints (source text remains copyrighted by Swiss authorities, only labels released) may complicate full reproducibility/reuse, since users must independently re-scrape and align the original documents.
